newsitem.title: USA: Earnings outlook behind U.S. stocks rise - Greenspan.
newsitem.headline: Earnings outlook behind U.S. stocks rise - Greenspan.

text.p: Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan said on Wednesday that the runup in U.S. stock prices can be explained by a favorable outlook for corporate earnings rather than by the infusion of cash from mutual funds.
"The market is being driven, not -- as best as I can judge -- by the large expansion of funds," Greenspan said in response to a question from the Senate Banking Committee.
Rather, he said, the market gains appear to be due to the "equity premium," or the expected rate of return on equities in comparison to less risky instruments such as Treasuries.

"The analytical breakdown of the (U.S. stock) market change in the last several years is explainable in terms of a dramatic increase in expected earnings growth over the long run and a decline in the risk premium," the Fed chief said in the first leg of his Humphrey-Hawkins testimony.
Greenspan said that history shows that while the flow of funds can affect stock prices in the short run, "in the long run the price is determined by how good a company it is."

The Fed official was also asked about his use of the phrase "irrational exuberance" in reference to markets. When he first used the phrase in a speech in December, he questioned whether such irrationality was affecting the markets, and he repeated the question in his formal testimony to Congress on Wednesday.
Greenspan said it was "very difficult" for policy makers to judge when markets have become irrational.
